title: Kuznets curve

definition.text: Simon Kuznets's hypothesis that, as an economy develops, market forces first raise and then lower economic inequality, tracing an inverted U.

facts.text: One explanation is that early industrialization draws cheap rural labour to cities, holding wages down while owners profit, before democratization and the welfare state spread the gains.
The hypothesis remains highly contested, with no consensus about its validity.
Inequality has risen in most developed countries since the 1960s, so the data no longer show the curve.
Kuznets himself warned the data were fragile and covered a very limited period, but other economists raised the curve 'to the level of law'.
The East Asian miracle, rapid growth in eight East Asian economies between 1965 and 1990 with falling poverty, has been used to challenge it.

contested_note: Economists have no consensus that inequality really rises then falls with development.

title: Environmental Kuznets curve

definition.text: The hypothesis that environmental damage gets worse as an economy grows until average income reaches a certain level, after which it improves.

facts.text: There is considerable evidence of the inverted-U pattern for some indicators such as water and air pollution, with pollutants like sulfur dioxide, lead and DDT cited.
Between 1970 and 2006 US real GDP grew 195% while sulfur dioxide emissions fell from 31 million tons to 15 million and lead emissions fell by more than 98%.
Net deforestation has ceased among countries with per capita GDP of at least $4,600, though rich countries may be 'exporting' deforestation.
Energy, land and resource use may not fall with rising income, and total energy use and many greenhouse gas emissions still rise in most developed countries.
Carbon may not follow the curve because, unlike local pollutants such as lead, cutting CO2 brings little local benefit, a tragedy of the commons.
Some researchers find an 'N' shape, with pollution rising again as income keeps growing, or argue pollution is simply exported to poorer countries.
It is a proposed model for eco-economic decoupling.

contested_note: Evidence supports the curve for some local pollutants, but its application to carbon, resource use and biodiversity is disputed.

title: Material Kuznets curve
article: Kuznets curve#Kuznets curves for steel and other metals

definition.text: The finding that a country's use of steel and other metals rises and then falls over its course of development, like a Kuznets curve.

facts.text: Steel production follows a Kuznets-type curve in economies including the United States, Japan, South Korea and China.
The terms 'Kuznets Curve for Steel' and 'Metal intensity Kuznets Curve' were first used by Huw McKay in 2008.

definition.text: The policy stance of being indifferent to GDP growth when designing policies for economic and social progress.

facts.text: Its reasoning is that GDP growth does not correlate closely with real progress.
In environmental policy it is opposed to both green growth and degrowth.
Economist Jeroen van den Bergh argues policy should neither chase nor avoid growth but directly use effective tools such as environmental taxes or emission rights to price externalities.
Whether the economy then grows, stagnates or shrinks is of secondary importance.

definition.text: An environmental philosophy that relies on advanced technology, social innovation, eco-innovation and sustainable design to solve environmental problems.

facts.text: It contrasts with environmentalism that calls for less consumption or simpler lifestyles.
Writer Alex Steffen coined the term in 2003.
Its core idea is that good communities, new technologies and sustainable living can raise quality of life while ecological footprints shrink.
Dark greens cite the Jevons paradox to argue technological approaches have limited benefits.

title: Dark, light and bright greens
article: Bright green environmentalism#Dark greens, light greens and bright greens

definition.text: Alex Steffen's three-way split of environmentalists into dark, light and bright greens.

facts.text: Light greens treat protecting the environment mainly as a personal responsibility and lifestyle choice.
Dark greens see environmental problems as built into industrial, capitalist civilization and its emphasis on growth, and seek radical change.
Bright greens also want radical change but believe better design, new technology and social innovation are the way to get it.

definition.text: In political and degrowth thought, the ability of people to act creatively and independently with others and their environment to meet their own needs.

facts.text: Ivan Illich introduced this meaning in his 1973 book Tools for Conviviality, as the opposite of industrial productivity that turns people into 'mere consumers'.
Convivial tools, such as most hand tools, bicycles and telephones, extend people's autonomy, unlike open-pit mines or road networks.
It is a core concept of degrowth, and degrowth writers generally accept that technologies suited to a degrowth society must be convivial.
Convivial tools resemble the 'intermediate technology' of E. F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful.

title: Degrowth in the Global South

definition.text: The study of whether and how degrowth ideas apply to the countries of the Global South.

facts.text: Applying degrowth there is debated, since many Southern countries still have unmet basic needs and may need some material growth.
Many of degrowth's roots lie in Southern traditions such as Buen Vivir in the Andes and Ubuntu in Southern Africa.
Some frame Northern degrowth as decolonization: shrinking the North's footprint to leave room for the South, linked to the idea of ecological debt.
Critics warn Northern degrowth could destabilize export-dependent Southern economies.

contested_note: Scholars disagree on whether degrowth suits countries that still need growth to meet basic needs.
